The Weakest Link Tells It All: Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via Learnable Credit Assignment

Abstract

Process reward models (PRMs) enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by providing fine-grained feedback, yet training PRMs typically requires expensive stepwise annotations. Outcome-supervised PRMs offer a scalable alternative by learning from final-answer correctness alone, but this introduces a fundamental credit assignment challenge, i.e., attributing outcomes to responsible reasoning steps. Existing approaches rely on either uniform or causal assignment, both of which fail to anchor credit in step correctness and thus hinder process error identification.

In this work, we propose Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via Learnable Credit Assignment (LCA), an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling under the principle of Weakest Link Assignment: a reasoning chain is as strong as its weakest link. To address mutual dependence between credit assignment and reward modeling, we formalize outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem and introduce Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, an MIL pooling technique tailored for strong dependence and redundancy among reasoning states. We prove Bayes consistency of our algorithm under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LCA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRMs across multiple tasks and backbones. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LCA.

1 Introduction

Process reward modeling (PRM) plays a crucial role in reasoning-intensive tasks for large language models (LLMs), such as mathematical problem-solving  Shao et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2024) and code generation Li et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025a). Unlike outcome reward models (ORMs)  Cobbe et al. (2021), which evaluate only the final answer , PRMs Wang et al. (2024c); Lightman et al. (2024); Luo et al. (2024) assess the correctness of each intermediate reasoning step, providing dense, step-level signals that enhance test-time scaling Wang et al. (2024c); Snell et al. (2025) and reinforcement learning Setlur et al. (2025); Cheng et al. (2026).

However, training PRMs requires step-level correctness labels, which are prohibitively expensive to collect from humans Lightman et al. (2024). A natural alternative is to use final-answer correctness, cheap to verify and widely available, as ground-truth supervision. To recover step-level rewards from this trajectory-level signal, one must solve a credit assignment problem: attributing trajectory-level correctness to the steps that cause it. This setting is termed outcome-supervised PRM.

Existing methods mainly fall into two perspectives.

  • •

    Uniform Assignment via Additive Aggregation: As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), this line Chen et al. (2025); Yuan et al. (2025) aggregates step-level scores by summation or averaging into a single trajectory score for optimization. Every step thus receives equal credit, regardless of which is actually responsible for the outcome.

  • •

    Causal Assignment via Rollout Estimation: As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), this line Wang et al. (2024c); Luo et al. (2024); Guan et al. (2025) pseudo-labels each step via Monte Carlo estimation of the probability of reaching a correct final answer. Each step’s score thus reflects the expected success of its downstream rollouts rather than its own correctness, making the actual error hard to localize. The estimation further depends on rollout policy and sampling design, which risks introducing bias and noise.

Both approaches share a common deficiency: neither attributes credit based on whether each step is actually correct. Uniform Assignment treats every step the same; Causal Assignment lets a step’s score depend on what comes after it. We propose to anchor credit assignment directly in step correctness, drawing on a long-standing intuition: a reasoning chain is only as strong as its weakest link Prasad et al. (2023); Jacovi et al. (2024); Li et al. (2023); Gilda and Gilda (2026). A chain is correct if and only if every step is correct, and incorrect if and only if any step is wrong. We term this Weakest Link Assignment (Figure 1(c)). Training under this principle directly targets the same first-error criterion widely adopted in PRM evaluation and applications Cheng et al. (2026); Lightman et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2025), thereby closing the training–test gap and producing a PRM that accurately attributes credit to the outcome-determining steps.

Yet applying this principle to training poses a chicken-and-egg dilemma: assigning credit to specific steps requires knowing which step is wrong, while identifying wrong steps is precisely what the PRM is being trained to do. Credit assignment and reward modeling are thus mutually dependent.

To resolve this challenge, we propose Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via Learnable Credit Assignment (LCA), an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling. Through a structural reduction, we formalize outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem Waqas et al. (2024): each trajectory prefix is an “instance”, the whole trajectory is a “bag” (i.e., a set of instances), and the Weakest Link principle is the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption verbatim. This formalization places outcome-supervised PRM within the principled MIL framework, which jointly learns instance classification and the bag-to-instance attribution under bag-level supervision, thereby dissolving the chicken-and-egg dilemma between credit assignment and reward modeling. Through Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, we resolve the degeneration of mainstream MIL methods under inter-instance dependence and redundancy, and embed a smoothed Weakest Link Assignment as a structural prior, yielding a learning objective that is Bayes consistent at the instance level.

To summarize, our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Insightfully, through a systematic analysis of existing outcome-supervised PRM methods, we identify a shared deficiency: neither Uniform Assignment nor Causal Assignment anchors credit in step correctness. We propose Weakest Link Assignment as a principled alternative, yielding PRMs that accurately attribute credit to the steps that cause the outcome.

  • •

    Technically, we propose LCA, an outcome-supervised PRM framework that (1) formalizes outcome-supervised credit assignment as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem under the Weakest Link principle; (2) introduces Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, an MIL pooling technique that adaptively reweights reasoning steps and embeds a smoothed Weakest Link Assignment as a structural prior, addressing the degeneration of mainstream MIL methods under inter-instance dependence and redundancy; and (3) proves Bayes consistency of the resulting learning objective at the instance level.

  • •

    Experimentally, on error identification and best-of-N test-time scaling, LCA consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRM baselines across multiple LLM backbones and generator models. Ablation studies further validate SWS pooling against widely used MIL pooling techniques and characterize the role of the temperature parameter.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Multiple Instance Learning

Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a weakly-supervised learning method designed for settings where only coarse-grained labels are available but fine-grained classification is required. MIL assumes a hierarchical structure of instances and bags. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the instance space. A bag BB is a finite set of instances xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}. The bag space is ℬ\mathcal{B}, with a data distribution ℙ\mathbb{P} over ℬ\mathcal{B}.

In the standard binary MIL setting, each instance and each bag has a label y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} (0 = negative, 1 = positive). Instance labels are unobserved; only bag labels are given. Given a training set D={⟨Bk,y⁡(Bk)⟩}k=1KD=\{\langle B^{k},y(B^{k})\rangle\}_{k=1}^{K} drawn from ℙ\mathbb{P}, the goal is to learn an instance-level classifier f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1].

Most MIL algorithms rely on the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption Foulds and Frank (2010):

Assumption 2.1 (Standard Multi-Instance Assumption).

A bag is positive if and only if it contains at least one positive instance:

y⁡(B)=max⁡{y⁡(x1),…,y⁡(xn)},\displaystyle y(B)=\max\{y(x_{1}),\dots,y(x_{n})\},
∀B={x1,…,xn}∈ℬ.\displaystyle\quad\forall B=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\in\mathcal{B}.

This assumption holds in many real-world applications, such as anomaly detection in long time series or whole-slide images (WSIs) Xu et al. (2014); Early et al. (2024). Anomalies typically appear in local regions, yet the label is assigned to the entire input. The goal of MIL in such cases is to pinpoint the anomaly location.

Modern MIL methods are predominantly pooling-based. These methods develop instance-level classifiers and use a pooling function to aggregate instance predictions into a bag-level prediction. Standard supervised learning optimizes the bag-level prediction, typically using a cross-entropy loss:

LC​E​(y⁡(B),Pool​({p1,…,pn})),\displaystyle L_{CE}\Big(y(B),\text{Pool}(\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\})\Big),

where p1,…,pnp_{1},\dots,p_{n} are instance predictions and Pool is the pooling function. In this way, instance classification and bag-to-instance attribution are jointly optimized in an end-to-end manner.

A more detailed discussion of MIL pooling techniques is deferred to Appendix B.

2.2 Process Reward Model

Reasoning trajectory.

A reasoning trajectory τ\tau consists of a question qq followed by a sequence of steps s1,…,sTs_{1},\dots,s_{T}:

τ:=⟨q,s1,…,sT⟩,\tau:=\langle q,s_{1},\dots,s_{T}\rangle,

where each step advances the reasoning based on the question and all previous steps.11 1 For clarity, we consider only sequential reasoning without self-correction in the main text. Our method naturally applies to reasoning with reflection and backtracking through a simple conceptual transformation; see Appendix E. An incomplete trajectory is termed a prefix:

τ:t:=⟨q,s1,…,st⟩,t≤T.\tau_{:t}:=\langle q,s_{1},\dots,s_{t}\rangle,\quad t\leq T.

Correctness of reasoning prefixes.

A reasoning step is logically erroneous if its conclusion is false or does not follow from the preceding context. Once such an error occurs, subsequent steps inherit the error, making their individual correctness ill-defined Lightman et al. (2024). We therefore assign correctness labels to prefixes rather than to isolated steps.

Formally, define correctness of a prefix τ:t\tau_{:t} as

y(τ:t)∈{0,1},y(\tau_{:t})\in\{0,1\},

where 11 denotes that τ:t\tau_{:t} contains logical error(s) (positive) and 00 denotes no error (negative), matching the standard MIL convention. By this definition, error monotonicity follows immediately:

y(τ:t+1)≥y(τ:t),y(\tau_{:t+1})\geq y(\tau_{:t}), (1)

because any extension of an erroneous prefix remains erroneous. The correctness of the full trajectory is thus

y(τ)=y(τ:T)=max{y(τ:1),…,y(τ:T)},y(\tau)=y(\tau_{:T})=\max\{y(\tau_{:1}),\dots,y(\tau_{:T})\}, (2)

which is precisely the Weakest Link Assignment.

Process reward modeling.

Process reward modeling learns a classifier ff that maps each prefix to a correctness score: f(τ:t)∈[0,1]f(\tau_{:t})\in[0,1], with the goal that f(τ:t)≈y(τ:t)f(\tau_{:t})\approx y(\tau_{:t}). This is equivalent to first-error detection Lightman et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2025): the first prefix for which ff signals an error identifies the earliest step that caused the failure.

3 Analysis

3.1 Process Reward Modeling as Multiple Instance Learning

Under the Weakest Link principle, we formalize outcome-supervised process reward modeling as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem:

  • •

    Data structure. A full trajectory τ\tau corresponds to a bag, and each prefix τ:t\tau_{:t} to an instance. We thus use “bag” and “trajectory” (resp. “instance” and “prefix”) interchangeably when the context is clear.

  • •

    Assumption. By the definition of prefix correctness, the bag-level label is the maximum over instance labels (Eq. 2); this exactly matches the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption.

  • •

    Learning objective. Given a dataset with trajectory-level labels: D={⟨τk,y⁡(τk)⟩}k=1KD=\{\langle\tau^{k},y(\tau^{k})\rangle\}_{k=1}^{K}, our goal is to learn a prefix-level classifier ff such that f(τ:t)≈y(τ:t)f(\tau_{:t})\approx y(\tau_{:t}), consistent with the paradigm of MIL.

Despite this formal alignment, outcome-supervised PRM raises a unique challenge absent in classic MIL: prefixes within a trajectory are both highly dependent and redundant, violating the common assumption of instance independence or weak dependence Waqas et al. (2024). This violation stems from three structural properties of reasoning trajectories:

  • •

    Autoregressive: each reasoning step is conditioned on all previous steps.

  • •

    Nested: each prefix includes previous ones.

  • •

    Monotonic: prefix labels are monotonic (Eq. 1).

Together, these three properties render each instance highly informative about the others. Most critically, the last prefix alone suffices to determine the bag label, making all earlier prefixes ignorable for bag-level classification.

Consequently, conventional MIL pooling techniques struggle in our setting. In preliminary experiments, we applied max-pooling-based MIL, the most direct realization of the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption. Yet the PRM rapidly degenerated into an ORM, producing meaningful predictions only at the final prefix while outputting a trivial value for all preceding prefixes. Detailed setup and results are provided in Appendix D.1. Attention-based MIL methods, though most prevalent in the deep learning era, are prone to a similar failure mode. The model could focus its attention exclusively on the last prefix, thus offering no guarantee of instance-level classification performance.

3.2 Multiple Instance Learning with Softmax-Weighted-Sum Pooling

To handle the strong dependence and redundancy among instances, we propose Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling. Given instance-level predictions 𝒑=(p1,…,pT)∈[0,1]T\bm{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{T})\in[0,1]^{T}, the bag-level prediction is

SWSα​(𝒑)=∑t=1Twt​pt,wt=ept/α∑j=1Tepj/α,\text{SWS}_{\alpha}(\bm{p})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}p_{t},\quad w_{t}=\frac{e^{p_{t}/\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{T}e^{p_{j}/\alpha}}, (3)

where the temperature α>0\alpha>0 controls the entropy of the weight distribution. As α→0\alpha\to 0, SWS approaches max pooling; as α→∞\alpha\to\infty, it approaches average pooling.

SWS pooling offers two key properties for our setting. First, because every weight wtw_{t} admits a strictly positive lower bound under bounded bag sizes, each instance is guaranteed to receive a non-negligible credit. This prevents the model from basing its predictions on an overly narrow subset of instances and thus promotes more generalizable instance classification. Second, the softmax weighting naturally encodes the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption as a structural prior: the weight of each instance grows with its predicted positivity, aligning with the Weakest Link Assignment where positive instances dominate the bag prediction.

SWS-pooling-based MIL provides an adaptive yet principled credit assignment mechanism. The model learns instance predictions ptp_{t}, which in turn determine the softmax weights wtw_{t} and thus each instance’s contribution to the bag-level loss. In this way, the model learns which instances drive the optimization objective under pure bag-level supervision, while the softmax-based architecture embeds the Standard MIL assumption to constrain the solution space.

3.3 Theoretical Analysis

We provide theoretical results about the Bayes consistency of SWS pooling. The analysis applies not only to our settings of outcome-supervised PRM but to any MIL setting that satisfies Assumption 3.1. We therefore adopt the general MIL notation introduced in Section 2.1.

Definition 3.1 (Bag cover set).

Let S⊆𝒳S\subseteq\mathcal{X} be a set of instances. The bag cover set of SS is the set of all bags that contain at least one instance from SS:

𝒞⁡(S):={B∈ℬ∣B∩S≠∅}.\mathcal{C}(S):=\{B\in\mathcal{B}\mid B\cap S\neq\emptyset\}.

Similarly, the positive bag cover set 𝒞+​(S)\mathcal{C}^{+}(S) is the set of all positive bags containing at least one instance from SS; the negative bag cover set 𝒞−​(S)\mathcal{C}^{-}(S) is defined analogously.

Assumption 3.1 (MM-Assumption).

There exists a constant M>0M>0 such that for any set SS of negative instances, if

ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))=ℙ⁡(𝒞+​(S))+ℙ⁡(𝒞−​(S))>0,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S))+\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S))>0,

then

ℙ​(𝒞+​(S))ℙ​(𝒞−​(S))≤M.\frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S))}{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S))}\leq M.

Assumption 3.1 is a mild assumption that prevents the probability ratio of a negative instance appearing in positive bags versus negative bags from being arbitrarily large.

Theorem 3.1 (Unique global minimizer).

Let Assumption 3.1 hold. Let NN be the maximum allowed bag size. Let f⁡(x)∈[0,1]f(x)\in[0,1] be an instance classifier. For a bag B=(x1,…,xn)B=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) with label y⁡(B)∈{0,1}y(B)\in\{0,1\}, define the softmax weighted sum

p^​(B)=SWSα​(f⁡(x1),⋯,f⁡(xn)),\hat{p}(B)=\text{SWS}_{\alpha}(f(x_{1}),\cdots,f(x_{n})),

and the expected loss

ℒ⁡(f)=𝔼B∼ℙ​LCE​(p^​(B),y⁡(B)).\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{B\sim\mathbb{P}}L_{\text{CE}}(\hat{p}(B),y(B)).

Then there exists a sufficiently small temperature α>0\alpha>0 such that, up to a set of instances SS whose bag cover set has probability zero, ℒ\mathcal{L} is uniquely minimized by the true label function:

f∗​(x)=y⁡(x)∈{0,1},∀x∉S.f^{*}(x)=y(x)\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall x\notin S.
Theorem 3.2 (Convergence in probability).

Let Assumption 3.1 hold. Let NN be the maximum allowed bag size. Let f∗​(x)=y​(x)f^{*}(x)=y(x) be the Bayes optimal classifier, and let {fl}\{f_{l}\} be a sequence of instance classifiers. Define the expected loss ℒ\mathcal{L} as in Theorem 3.1. Then there exists a sufficiently small temperature α>0\alpha>0 such that, if {ℒ⁡(fl)}\{\mathcal{L}(f_{l})\} converges to ℒ⁡(f∗)\mathcal{L}(f^{*}):

liml→∞ℒ⁡(fl)=arg⁡minf⁡ℒ⁡(f)=ℒ⁡(f∗),\lim_{l\to\infty}\mathcal{L}(f_{l})=\arg\min_{f}\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathcal{L}(f^{*}),

then {fl}\{f_{l}\} converges to f∗f^{*} in probability.

Together, Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 guarantee a desirable property of SWS-pooling-based MIL algorithms: by minimizing the expected loss ℒ\mathcal{L}, the instance classifier ff approximates the Bayes optimal classifier f∗f^{*}. Consequently, even without instance-level supervision, the learned classifier is expected to perform well on instance classification.

Our theoretical analysis reveals the central role of temperature α\alpha in SWS pooling. Intuitively, a larger α\alpha makes the credit assignment more uniform, risking misclassification of negative instances that frequently appear in positive bags. So Bayes consistency requires α\alpha to be sufficiently small, as stated in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. On the other hand, however, an excessively small α\alpha concentrates the credit assignment on a single instance, thereby starving co-occurring positive instances of adequate optimization signals. Consequently, the choice of α\alpha involves a trade-off between theoretical soundness and empirical effectiveness.

A more formal statement of the definitions, assumptions, theorems, and their detailed proofs can be found in Appendix F.

4 Method

Building on the above analysis, we propose LCA, an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling via SWS-pooling-based MIL algorithm. Figure 2 illustrates the overall pipeline.

We adopt the standard discriminative PRM architecture Zheng et al. (2026), which appends a binary classification head to a pretrained LLM backbone. Given a full reasoning trajectory τ=⟨q,s1,…,sT⟩\tau=\langle q,s_{1},\dots,s_{T}\rangle, the LLM backbone ℳ\mathcal{M} extracts per-prefix representations in a single forward pass and the classification head ψ\psi outputs the predicted error probability for each prefix:

f⁡(τ)=ψ⁡(ℳ⁡(τ))=(p1,…,pT)∈[0,1]T,f(\tau)=\psi(\mathcal{M}(\tau))=(p_{1},\dots,p_{T})\in[0,1]^{T}, (4)

where ptp_{t} denotes the probability that prefix τ:t\tau_{:t} is incorrect.

We then aggregate these prefix-level predictions into a trajectory-level score using SWS pooling:

p^​(τ)=SWSα​(𝒑)=SWSα​(p1,⋯,pT).\hat{p}(\tau)=\text{SWS}_{\alpha}(\bm{p})=\text{SWS}_{\alpha}(p_{1},\cdots,p_{T}). (5)

We train the PRM end-to-end by minimizing the empirical cross-entropy loss at trajectory level:

ℒ^K\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{K} =1K​∑k=1KLC​E​(p^​(τk),y⁡(τk))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}L_{CE}\bigl(\hat{p}(\tau^{k}),y(\tau^{k})\bigr) (6)
=−1K∑k=1K(y(τk)logp^(τk)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl(y(\tau^{k})\log\hat{p}(\tau^{k})
OPEN+(1−y⁡(τk))​log⁡(1−p^​(τk))).\displaystyle+(1-y(\tau^{k}))\log(1-\hat{p}(\tau^{k}))\Bigr).

where y⁡(τk)∈{0,1}y(\tau^{k})\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the final answer is correct (00) or incorrect (11). No step-level supervision is required. In practice, we apply a stop-gradient operation to the softmax weights wtw_{t} to stabilize training.

5 Experiments

We conduct a series of experiments to answer four research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Can PRMs trained with LCA reliably locate errors in reasoning trajectories?

  • •

    RQ2: Can PRMs trained with LCA enhance LLM reasoning capability via test-time scaling?

  • •

    RQ3: How does the temperature α\alpha affect SWS pooling’s performance?

  • •

    RQ4: Does SWS pooling outperform other pooling techniques on process reward modeling?

Our experiments focus on math reasoning, where the correctness of intermediate steps and final answers is relatively well-defined and easy to verify. Unless otherwise stated, we use the correctness of the final answer as the trajectory-level label, without any process-level annotation.

Implementation details for all experiments are given in Appendix C.

5.1 Experiments on Error Identification (RQ1)

Datasets and Models. We use the publicly available Math-Shepherd dataset Wang et al. (2024c) as training set. Though this dataset provides step-level labels generated by Monte Carlo estimation, we discard these process labels and use only the problems and their final answers for LCA. We use Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct Yang et al. (2024) and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct Grattafiori et al. (2024) as the LLM backbone for training PRMs.

Evaluation Metrics. We use ProcessBench Zheng et al. (2025) to measure the PRM’s ability to identify the first error location in a response. The benchmark evaluates recognition of fully correct responses and precise error identification in incorrect responses. We calculate accuracies on correct and erroneous samples and report their harmonic mean as the final F1 score.

Baselines. We compare our method with the current state-of-the-art baselines:

  • •

    ImplicitPRM Yuan et al. (2025) parameterizes the reward model as a log-likelihood ratio of policy and reference models, training with trajectory-level correctness labels.

  • •

    MathShepherd Wang et al. (2024c) uses brute-force Monte Carlo estimation to generate hard pseudo labels for every step.

  • •

    SCAN Ding et al. (2026) denoises Monte Carlo pseudo labels using the confidence of the data generator.

  • •

    OmegaPRM Luo et al. (2024) uses Monte Carlo tree search to selectively generate high-quality reasoning trajectories with soft pseudo labels.

  • •

    PQM Li and Li (2025) formulates process reward modeling as a Q-value ranking problem and trains PRMs with a ranking loss, which requires estimation of the first error location.

We also incorporate several 7B-scale open-source PRMs and LLM-as-critic models as baselines; their results are taken directly from previous research Zhang et al. (2025b).

Main Results.

Table 1 reports evaluation results on ProcessBench. Our method achieves strong performance, outperforming the second-best by 21.7% on the 3B backbone and 5.5% on the 7B backbone. On the 7B backbone, LCA surpasses all baselines and establishes a new state of the art. On the 3B backbone, LCA outperforms all competing 3B methods by a substantial margin. Notably, our method avoids the heavy computational cost of Monte Carlo sampling required by MathShepherd, SCAN, OmegaPRM and PQM, yet consistently surpasses them in performance.

More detailed results can be found in Table 4 in Appendix D.2.

5.2 Experiments on Test-Time Scaling (RQ2)

Datasets and Models. We train PRMs on the Math-Shepherd dataset, using Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct as the backbone. We evaluate test-time scaling on MATH-500 Lightman et al. (2024), a subset of MATH dataset. To test generalizability, we select three generator models of different sizes, families, and reasoning capabilities: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 Jiang et al. (2023), Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct Grattafiori et al. (2024), and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Qwen et al. (2025).

Evaluation Metrics. Following prior work Wang et al. (2024c); Lightman et al. (2024); Luo et al. (2024), we evaluate PRMs by their verification ability using best-of-N sampling. The metric BON@n measures the correctness of the most preferred trajectory selected by the PRM from nn candidates per question.

Baselines. We compare our method with the same baselines as in Section 5.1: ImplicitPRM, MathShepherd, SCAN, OmegaPRM, and PQM.

Main Results. Table 2 reports the best-of-N performance for N=8N=8, 3232, and 6464. Our method achieves the highest average score across generators. Moreover, LCA attains the best results on all three generation models at N=32N=32 and N=64N=64, demonstrating strong scalability and generalization. Although our method is primarily designed for intra-trajectory credit assignment rather than for validating the final answer, it still delivers consistent gains on best-of-N accuracy. We attribute this to the Weakest Link Assignment, which anchors credit assignment directly in step correctness. Therefore, the PRM learns to focus on per-step correctness instead of relying on spurious correlations or shortcuts, which mitigates overfitting and improves generalization.

5.3 Ablation Study (RQ3&4)

We conduct ablation studies to examine the effect of temperature α\alpha and the advantage of SWS pooling over other common MIL pooling techniques.

Effect of Temperature(RQ3).

Following the settings of our main experiments, we train PRMs with different α\alpha using Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct as backbone and Math-Shepherd as training set, and report their F1 scores on ProcessBench splits.

Figure 3 shows the results. As α\alpha increases, performance on GSM8K decreases, while performance on OlympiadBench and OmniMath increases. This finding aligns with our theoretical insights. A larger α\alpha makes credit assignment more uniform across instances, which encourages the model to identify as many positive instances as possible within a positive bag, and thus benefits process error detection. However, this also risks misclassifying negative instances that appear in positive bags, e.g., correct prefixes of eventually wrong trajectories. Consequently, as α\alpha increases, performance drops on simple datasets with fewer process errors (e.g., GSM8K) but improves on complex datasets with substantial process errors (e.g., OlympiadBench and OmniMath) Zhang et al. (2025b). This again highlights that choosing α\alpha requires a trade-off between theoretical consistency and practical effectiveness.

Comparing SWS Pooling with Other Pooling Techniques (RQ4).

We compare SWS pooling against commonly used MIL pooling functions: instance pooling Wang et al. (2018), embedding pooling Tibo et al. (2018), attention pooling Ilse et al. (2018), and conjunctive pooling Jang and Kwon (2025). Appendix B describes these techniques in detail. We also include a fully supervised PRM that uses all step-level ground-truth labels as an upper bound baseline. To avoid potential label noise and ensure consistency with standard MIL settings, we curate a training set from the human-annotated PRM800K dataset Lightman et al. (2024) and aggregate step labels to obtain trajectory labels (see Appendix C.5 for details). We use Qwen3-4B Yang et al. (2025) as the backbone to train PRMs.

Figure 4 reports the average F1 scores on ProcessBench. SWS pooling with temperature α=0.2\alpha=0.2 achieves the best score, surpassing other pooling techniques and closely matching the stepwise-supervised baseline. Temperatures higher or lower than 0.2 yield suboptimal performance, while the optimal temperature depends on data and model.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we present a systematic analysis of outcome-supervised process reward modeling from the perspective of credit assignment, identifying the fundamental limitation of existing uniform and causal assignment strategies. To address this, we propose Weakest Link Assignment as a principled alternative and introduce LCA, an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling. By formulating outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem and introducing Softmax-Weighted-Sum pooling, we resolve the chicken-and-egg dilemma between credit assignment and reward modeling under strong inter-instance dependence and redundancy. Both theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of LCA, offering a principled alternative for fine-grained process supervision in complex reasoning tasks.

Limitations

Despite achieving state-of-the-art performance among outcome-supervised process reward modeling methods, our approach still lags behind PRMs trained on human-annotated step-level labels. This gap highlights room for further improvement in weakly supervised reward modeling.

Furthermore, using final answer correctness as a proxy for trajectory-level labels may introduce inherent noise. LLMs sometimes arrive at the correct answer via flawed reasoning, in which case the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption does not strictly hold. While our method proves robust in practice, integrating techniques for learning with noisy labels into the MIL framework is a promising direction for future work.

Beyond the above, integrating PRMs into reinforcement learning (RL) remains another important open problem. PRM-guided RL is susceptible to reward hacking, making this a non-trivial challenge. Existing explorations include reward design, optimization algorithms, and co-evolution of the reward model with the policy model. Notably, our method requires only outcome supervision to train PRMs and incurs no additional Monte Carlo sampling overhead, rendering it particularly suitable for reward-policy co-evolution. We see this as a valuable avenue for future investigation.

Ethical Considerations

All experiments in this work were carried out on publicly available datasets, models, and benchmarks, following their respective licenses and usage terms. The study does not involve human or animal subjects, and we did not collect, use, or disclose any personally identifiable information.

In this work, Large Language Models (LLMs) were used for language polishing and coding assistance. Specifically, LLMs supported refining the clarity and grammar of the manuscript, improving stylistic quality, and suggesting code snippets or troubleshooting strategies. All content generated by LLMs was carefully reviewed and verified by the authors before inclusion. The research design, critical analyses, and all final decisions were independently conducted by the authors. LLMs were not involved in generating new research ideas or conclusions.

Appendix A Related Work

A.1 Multiple Instance Learning

Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a weakly supervised learning paradigm in which labels are assigned to bags of instances rather than to individual instances. The task is to predict instance labels from bag labels alone. MIL has been applied to medical image analysis, text processing, time-series analysis, and video anomaly detection Xu et al. (2014); Angelidis and Lapata (2018); Early et al. (2024); Tian et al. (2021); Jang and Kwon (2025). To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply MIL to process reward modeling.

In the deep learning era, most MIL methods are pooling-based. Proposed pooling techniques include instance pooling Wang et al. (2018), embedding pooling Tibo et al. (2018), attention pooling Javed et al. (2022); Shao et al. (2021), additive pooling Javed et al. (2022), max pooling Liu et al. (2025), and conjunctive pooling Early et al. (2024); Angelidis and Lapata (2018); Jang and Kwon (2025). The use of softmax operation as pooling functions remains largely unexplored. The only prior work, an early study on sound event detection Salamon et al. (2017), employs a non-parametric softmax and has seen little subsequent adoption in the MIL literature. In this work, we propose Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, parameterized by a temperature α\alpha and tailored for bags with interdependent instances. Our theoretical analysis and experiments both demonstrate the crucial role of this hyperparameter for instance-level learnability.

A.2 Process Reward Models

Reward models are essential for improving large language models (LLMs) in complex reasoning tasks such as mathematical problem-solving Grattafiori et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2024) and competitive programming Hui et al. (2024). Unlike outcome reward models (ORMs), which evaluate only the final answer, process reward models (PRMs) Uesato et al. (2022); Lightman et al. (2024) assess each reasoning step, providing finer-grained feedback. Recent advancements Wang et al. (2024c); Luo et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024a) have demonstrated the significant potential of PRMs in scaling test-time compute Setlur et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025b) and post-training Guan et al. (2025); Cheng et al. (2026).

The main difficulty in training a PRM is obtaining reliable step-level annotations. Human annotation Lightman et al. (2024) is the primary source but is expensive and does not scale. Monte Carlo methods Wang et al. (2024c); Luo et al. (2024); Guan et al. (2025); Ding et al. (2026) offer a promising alternative, estimating a step’s quality by the empirical probability of reaching a correct final answer from that step. We refer to this as causal credit assignment: a step’s score reflects the expected success of its downstream completions rather than its own logical validity. This coupling causes errors from later steps to be incorrectly attributed to earlier ones, making it difficult to localize the true error source. Moreover, the estimates depend crucially on the choice of rollout policy and sampling strategy, which introduces noise and hampers generalization. Another line of research Yuan et al. (2025); Cui et al. (2025) adopts DPO-style implicit reward functions Rafailov et al. (2023), which are trained as ORMs but used as PRMs. Because the trajectory-level score decomposes into a sum over steps, this approach implicitly enforces uniform credit assignment: every step within the same trajectory receives the same optimization pressure, regardless of its actual contribution to the outcome. As a consequence, the model cannot differentiate genuinely erroneous steps from correct precursor steps, limiting its capacity for precise error identification. Moreover, these implicit reward functions are known to suffer from limited generalization Razin et al. (2026).

In this work, we advocate Weakest Link Assignment as a principled alternative, drawing on the long-standing intuition: a reasoning chain is correct if and only if every step is correct, and incorrect if and only if any step is wrong. This principle already underlies standard PRM evaluation and downstream usage: ProcessBench Zheng et al. (2025) evaluates PRMs via first-error detection; best-of-N sampling Lightman et al. (2024) typically aggregates step scores by taking the minimum (for scalar rewards) or the product (for probabilities); and recent work has shown that a min-form reward aggregation in reinforcement learning substantially reduces reward hackingCheng et al. (2026). Building on this, we propose an outcome-supervised process reward modeling framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling under the Weakest Link principle, thereby closing the training–test gap and producing a PRM that accurately attributes credit to the outcome-determining steps.

Appendix B Pooling Techniques in Multiple Instance Learning

This appendix provides a concise overview of the pooling techniques mentioned in this paper. We assume a standard deep MIL architecture: given a bag B={x1,…,xn}B=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}, a feature extractor ϕ\phi (e.g., a neural network backbone) maps each instance to a dd-dimensional embedding zi=ϕ⁡(xi)∈ℝdz_{i}=\phi(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. A classification head ψ\psi then produces instance-level predictions pi∈[0,1]p_{i}\in[0,1]. The pooling function aggregates the instance-level information to yield a bag-level prediction y^​(B)\hat{y}(B).

We describe six pooling methods commonly used in the MIL literature.

B.1 Embedding Pooling

Embedding pooling aggregates instance embeddings before classification. The bag embedding is obtained by averaging the instance embeddings:

zbag=1n​∑i=1nzi,z_{\text{bag}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i},

and the bag-level prediction is then y^​(B)=ψ​(zbag)\hat{y}(B)=\psi(z_{\text{bag}}). This approach is simple and widely used for bag-level classification, but it does not produce instance-level predictions and can lose discriminative instance information.

B.2 Instance Pooling

Instance pooling performs classification on each instance independently, then aggregates the resulting instance predictions. The bag-level prediction is the average of the instance probabilities:

pi=ψ⁡(zi),y^​(B)=1n​∑i=1npi.p_{i}=\psi(z_{i}),\qquad\hat{y}(B)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}.

Instance pooling naturally yields instance-level predictions, but the uniform averaging does not discriminate between more and less relevant instances.

B.3 Max Pooling

Max pooling selects the maximum instance prediction as the bag-level prediction:

y^​(B)=max⁡{p1,…,pn}.\hat{y}(B)=\max\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}.

This directly implements the standard multi-instance assumption: a bag is positive if at least one instance is positive. However, it assigns all credit to a single instance, which can lead to unstable training and poor generalization.

B.4 Attention Pooling

Attention pooling learns instance-specific weights via an attention mechanism, then aggregates the instance embeddings accordingly. An attention head ω\omega computes normalized attention weights:

ai=exp⁡(ω⁡(zi))∑j=1nexp⁡(ω⁡(zj)),a_{i}=\frac{\exp(\omega(z_{i}))}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(\omega(z_{j}))},

and the bag-level prediction is y^​(B)=ψ⁡(∑i=1nai​zi)\hat{y}(B)=\psi\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}z_{i}\right). This method allows learnable, instance-specific weighting, but the attention weights are not directly constrained by the standard multi-instance assumption, which can lead to degenerate solutions.

B.5 Additive Pooling

Additive pooling combines attention pooling and instance pooling. Instance embeddings are first scaled by their attention weights before classification:

ai=exp⁡(ω⁡(zi))∑j=1nexp⁡(ω⁡(zj)),pi=ψ⁡(ai​zi).a_{i}=\frac{\exp(\omega(z_{i}))}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(\omega(z_{j}))},\qquad p_{i}=\psi(a_{i}z_{i}).

The bag-level prediction is then:

y^​(B)=1n​∑i=1npi.\hat{y}(B)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}.

This hybrid approach encourages the model to attend to relevant instances while still performing instance-level classification.

B.6 Conjunctive Pooling

Conjunctive pooling computes attention weights and instance predictions independently, then combines them multiplicatively:

ai=exp⁡(ω⁡(zi))∑j=1nexp⁡(ω⁡(zj)),pi=ψ⁡(zi).a_{i}=\frac{\exp(\omega(z_{i}))}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(\omega(z_{j}))},\qquad p_{i}=\psi(z_{i}).

The bag-level prediction is:

y^​(B)=1n​∑i=1nai​pi.\hat{y}(B)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}p_{i}.

By training the attention and classification heads in parallel, this method avoids the potential degeneracy where the classifier relies on the attention head to pre-process the input, making the model more robust.

B.7 Discussion

Despite the empirical success of MIL across diverse applications, most common pooling techniques lack theoretical guarantees for instance-level classification accuracy. Attention-based pooling, currently the most widely used approach, has been shown not to be PAC-learnable Jang and KWON (2024). Average-pooling methods do not align with the multi-instance assumption. Max-pooling, while most consistent with the assumption, suffers from low sample efficiency and training instability, which limits its practical adoption.

In contrast, our proposed temperature-parameterized SWS pooling exhibits a favorable property—instance-level Bayes consistency of the learning objective—under mild assumptions, and performs well in outcome-supervised PRM tasks. However, we note that the bag sizes in our setting are modest (typically under a few dozen), whereas some MIL applications involve bags with hundreds to thousands of instances Zheng et al. (2024). Whether SWS pooling remains effective in such large-bag regimes is uncertain and lies outside the scope of this work.

Appendix C Dataset and Implementation Details

C.1 Dataset Details

We provide details of the datasets and benchmarks used in this work.

  • •

    Math-Shepherd Wang et al. (2024c)22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/peiyi9979/Math-Shepherd serves as the training set in our main experiments (Sections 5.1 and 5.2). It contains 445k English math reasoning trajectories with their associated problems. Each reasoning step is labeled via Monte Carlo (MC) estimation without human annotation; the MC rollouts are not included. We use the entire dataset for training and do not perform evaluation on it.

  • •

    PRM800K Lightman et al. (2024)33 3 https://github.com/openai/prm800k is used as the training set for the ablation study on pooling techniques (Section 5.3). The dataset comprises roughly 40k English math reasoning trajectories and their problems. Human annotators label the location of the first error in each trajectory. We adopt the original train/test split, yielding 37.5k training and 3.7k test trajectories. The training split is further processed as described in Appendix C.5; the test split is not used for evaluation.

  • •

    MATH-500 Lightman et al. (2024)44 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500provides the problem set for best-of-N evaluation (Section 5.2). It is a subset of the MATH dataset Hendrycks et al. (2021) comprising 500 English math problems. We use all 500 problems as the test set.

  • •

    ProcessBench Zheng et al. (2025)55 5 https://huggingface.co/datasets/Qwen/ProcessBench is the evaluation benchmark for our main experiments (Section 5.1). It consists of four splits—GSM8K (0.4k), MATH (1k), OlympiadBench (1k), and Omni-MATH (1k)—which differ in difficulty. Each problem comes with a reasoning chain, and all text is in English. Every trajectory is manually annotated with the first error location. We evaluate on all four splits. Evaluation details are given in Appendix C.4.

C.2 PRM Training Details

Model architecture.

For our method(LCA), MathShepherd Wang et al. (2024c), OmegaPRM Luo et al. (2024), and SCANDing et al. (2026), we remove the language modeling head from the LLM backbone and initialize a randomly initialized classification head, implemented as a two-layer MLP with the same hidden dimension as the LLM backbone. ImplicitPRMYuan et al. (2025) uses the log-probability ratio between the policy model and the reference model (the same LLM backbone without fine-tuning) as an implicit reward model. For PQMLi and Li (2025), we replace the language modeling head with a linear value head following the original paper.

Hyperparameters.

For Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct backbones, we set the learning rate to 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}; for the Qwen3-4B backbone, we use 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}. All experiments employ a linear learning rate scheduler. For all methods except PQM, we use a global batch size (GPU count × gradient accumulation steps × per-GPU batch size) of 384 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct backbones, and 512 on Qwen3-4B. For PQM, we adopt the more fine-grained batching strategy described in its original paperLi and Li (2025). All models are trained for a single epoch.

Infrastructure.

All experiments are conducted on four 80GB A800 GPUs using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 parallel trainingRasley et al. (2020).

C.3 Baseline Implementation Details

MathShepherd, PQM, and ImplicitPRM are trained directly on the Math-Shepherd dataset. For ImplicitPRM, we use cross-entropy loss with β=0.05\beta=0.05. For PQM, we set ζ=2\zeta=2. Other implement details follow the original papers.

OmegaPRM and SCAN improve the data collection and labeling strategy on top of MathShepherd and thus cannot be trained directly on the Math-Shepherd dataset. We therefore generate training data following their respective proposals. To ensure a fair comparison, we use the same set of problems as in Math-Shepherd dataset and adopt MetaMath-Llemma-7BYu et al. (2024) as the generator model, which is used for Monte Carlo rollouts in Math-Shepherd dataset. For both methods, the amount of generated data is comparable to that of Math-Shepherd.

For OmegaPRM, as no official code is available, we use the open-source implementation openr66 6 https://github.com/openreasoner/openrWang et al. (2024b) for MCTS-based data generation. We set the search limit to 200 per question, α=0.5\alpha=0.5, β=0.9\beta=0.9, L=500L=500, and cpuct=0.125c_{\text{puct}}=0.125. For each Monte Carlo estimation, we sample k=16k=16 rollouts. See the original paper for detailsWang et al. (2024a).

For SCAN, we follow the proposed denoising procedure on top of the Math-Shepherd dataset, with a tolerant distance d=2d=2. For each problem, we first generate k=16k=16 rollouts to estimate the confidence of the completor model. For each trajectory in the dataset, we locate the first error (with label =0=0), then consider the first and second steps before that error, generate k=8k=8 completions for each, compute the Monte Carlo value, and combine it with the problem-level confidence to produce denoised labels. See the original paper for detailsDing et al. (2026).

C.4 Evaluation Details

ProcessBench evaluation.

We follow the evaluation protocol of ProcessBenchZheng et al. (2025). For our method(LCA), MathShepherd, and SCAN, PRMs are trained as standard binary classifiers; we therefore extract the earliest erroneous step directly from its correctness predictions for reasoning steps. OmegaPRM, ImplicitPRM, and PQM produce scalar scores for each step; we first transform these scores into binary correctness predictions using a threshold. The threshold is chosen as the one that yields the highest F1 score on the MATH subset (see Table 3).

Best-of-N evaluation.

We use Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the generator models to produce evaluation data for best-of-N sampling on the MATH500 problem set. The data for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct are taken directly from Yuan et al. (2025). For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we collect 64 rollouts per problem in MATH500 using temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, and a maximum generation length of 10241024. For binary classification models (LCA, MathShepherd, SCAN), we take the product of the step-wise scores as the trajectory score, consistent with earlier studies Lightman et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025b). For models that output real-valued scores (OmegaPRM, ImplicitPRM, PQM), we take the minimum of the step-wise scores, following their original papers.

C.5 Detailed Settings of Ablation on Pooling Techniques

We implement embedding pooling, instance pooling, attention pooling, and conjunctive pooling following the descriptions in Appendix B. For attention and conjunctive pooling, the attention head is realized as a simple linear value head, as the attention-based LLM backbone already provides sufficient nonlinearity.

As noted in Limitations, using final answer correctness as bag-level labels may introduce label noise when correct answers are reached through flawed reasoning, violating the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption. To eliminate this confounding factor and adhere strictly to the standard MIL setting, we construct a training set from the human-annotated PRM800K dataset Lightman et al. (2024). This dataset marks the first error location for each trajectory (−1-1 for error-free trajectories). We derive trajectory-level labels by checking whether the trajectory contains any error, and then discard the original step-level annotations. The resulting dataset is further balanced to ensure equal proportions of erroneous and correct trajectories, yielding a final set of 30k trajectories (50% containing errors), which we refer to as PRM800K-balanced. We then train PRMs on this dataset with different pooling techniques, using Qwen3-4B as the backbone. Training details are provided in Appendix C.2.

For the stepwise-supervised baseline, we retain the step-level labels from PRM800K-balanced. Steps before the annotated first error are labeled correct; all others are labeled incorrect. The PRM is trained with step-level cross-entropy loss, with all other settings unchanged.

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 Preliminary Experiments

In early experiments, we applied max pooling as the MIL aggregation mechanism, since it directly instantiates the Standard Multi-Instance Assumption. Using Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct as the backbone, we trained a PRM on the Math-Shepherd dataset. However, the PRM rapidly degenerated and performed poorly on downstream evaluations. Figure 5 shows the average prediction values of the resulting PRM across different relative positions in erroneous reasoning trajectories (0 denotes the first step, 1 the last step). The predictions remain near zero for all early positions but rise sharply at the final step. Figure 6 shows that the performance first improves and then collapses during training. This confirms our hypothesis that the strong dependence and redundancy among prefixes cause the classifier to quickly settle into degenerate solutions, failing to learn robust instance-level classification. In contrast, our proposed SWS pooling is provably Bayes consistent under mild assumptions and thus avoids such degenerate optima.

D.2 Full Results of ProcessBench Evaluation

We provide full results of ProcessBench evaluation in Table 4.

D.3 Case Studies

We show some qualatative examples taken from ProcessBench in Table 6. The blue values represent the predicted probability of incorrect provided by the PRM trained with LCA. The probability is high once encountering the first wrong step.

Appendix E Extension to Reasoning with Reflection and Backtracking

In the main text, we restrict our discussion to sequential reasoning without reflection or backtracking. Under this setting, any logical error, once introduced, is inherited by all subsequent steps and ultimately leads to an incorrect final answer. The Weakest Link principle therefore holds: a chain is correct iff every step is correct, and incorrect iff any step contains an error.

For reasoning that allows reflection and backtracking, however, a later step may correct an earlier mistake. Consequently, a trajectory that arrives at a correct final answer may temporarily contain intermediate errors, violating the Weakest Link principle in its strict sequential form. Below, we show that by lifting the formulation from linear prefixes to graph-structured reasoning states, sequential reasoning and reasoning with reflection can be treated within a unified framework, and our method applies seamlessly to both.

Reasoning state.

A reasoning state is a directed acyclic graph (DAG)

G=(𝒱,ℰ),G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}),

where each node v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} represents a premise, an intermediate conclusion, or the final answer, and each directed edge (u→v)∈ℰ(u\to v)\in\mathcal{E} indicates that vv is logically derived from uu.

Correctness of reasoning states.

A reasoning state GG is said to contain an error if there exists a node whose stated result is factually false or cannot be validly inferred from its parent nodes. We define the correctness label of GG as

y⁡(G)∈{0,1},y(G)\in\{0,1\},

where 11 denotes the presence of at least one logical error and 00 denotes an error-free state. Under this definition, correctness is monotone with respect to graph extension:

G1⊆G2⟹y⁡(G2)≥y⁡(G1),G_{1}\subseteq G_{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;y(G_{2})\geq y(G_{1}), (7)

since any error present in a subgraph G1G_{1} is inherited by every supergraph G2G_{2} that extends it.

Reasoning as graph construction.

A reasoning process can be viewed as the step-by-step construction of a reasoning state, starting from the initial premises and adding, modifying, or deleting nodes and edges until a node representing the final answer is produced.

For sequential reasoning without reflection, each step adds new nodes and edges to the current graph without removing any existing ones. Hence, every prefix of the trajectory corresponds to a subgraph of the subsequent prefix, and the monotonicity of prefix correctness (Eq. 1) follows immediately as a special case of Eq. 7.

For reasoning with reflection or backtracking, a step may revise or retract earlier conclusions, i.e., it may delete nodes or edges. In this case, earlier reasoning states are not necessarily subgraphs of later ones. Nevertheless, the monotonicity relation G1⊆G2⇒y⁡(G2)≥y⁡(G1)G_{1}\subseteq G_{2}\Rightarrow y(G_{2})\geq y(G_{1}) still holds for any pair where G1G_{1} is a subgraph of G2G_{2}.

Applying our PRM to reasoning with reflection.

Our method, LCA, trains the PRM on sequential reasoning trajectories and thus learns a classifier ff that maps a reasoning state to its error probability:

f⁡(G)∈[0,1],f(G)\in[0,1],

with the objective f⁡(G)≈y⁡(G)f(G)\approx y(G). Given a trajectory with reflection τ=⟨q,s1,…,sT⟩\tau=\langle q,s_{1},\dots,s_{T}\rangle, we first convert each prefix τ:t\tau_{:t} into its corresponding reasoning state GtG_{t} (the DAG constructed up to step tt) and linearize GtG_{t} into a sequential form, i.e., a prefix without backtracking. We then evaluate f⁡(Gt)f(G_{t}) for each step.

The step-wise quality of reasoning can be assessed by the change in the corretness of reasoning states:

  • •

    If f⁡(Gt)<f⁡(Gt−1)f(G_{t})<f(G_{t-1}), step tt improves the reasoning state (e.g., by correcting an earlier mistake).

  • •

    If f⁡(Gt)>f⁡(Gt−1)f(G_{t})>f(G_{t-1}), step tt introduces or amplifies an error.

  • •

    If f⁡(Gt)≈f⁡(Gt−1)f(G_{t})\approx f(G_{t-1}), step tt is neutral.

Thus, although trained solely on sequential trajectories without reflection, our PRM provides fine-grained, per-step feedback for reasoning with reflection and backtracking without any architectural modification.

Appendix F Proof of Theorems

F.1 Formulations and Assumptions

Definition F.1 (Instance space).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote the instance space. Each instance x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} is associated with a label

y⁡(x)∈{0,1},y(x)\in\{0,1\},

which induces a partition of 𝒳\mathcal{X} into the positive instance set and the negative instance set:

𝒳+:={x∈𝒳∣y⁡(x)=1},\displaystyle\mathcal{X}^{+}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid y(x)=1\},
𝒳−:={x∈𝒳∣y⁡(x)=0}.\displaystyle\mathcal{X}^{-}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid y(x)=0\}.
Definition F.2 (Bag space).

A bag (or multi-instance) BB is defined as a finite set of instances from 𝒳\mathcal{X}:

B=(x1,x2,…,xn),xi∈𝒳,1≤n≤N,B=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}),\quad x_{i}\in\mathcal{X},\quad 1\leq n\leq N,

where NN is the maximum allowed bag size. The bag space ℬ\mathcal{B} is the set of all possible bags:

ℬ=⋃n=1N𝒳n.\mathcal{B}=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}\mathcal{X}^{n}.

Each bag BB is associated with a label y⁡(B)∈{0,1}y(B)\in\{0,1\}, defined via the instance labels:

y⁡(B)=𝟏​(∃i∈{1,…,n}​ s.t. ​y​(xi)=1),y(B)=\mathbf{1}\Big(\exists i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\text{ s.t. }y(x_{i})=1\Big),

i.e., a bag is labeled positive if it contains at least one positive instance, and negative otherwise.

Definition F.3 (Bag distribution).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the bag space as defined above. A bag distribution is a probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P} on ℬ\mathcal{B} that describes how bags are generated. In general, the generation process can be described in two steps:

  1. 1.

    The bag size nn is drawn from a discrete distribution over {1,2,…,N}\{1,2,\dots,N\}:

    n∼PN​(n),n\sim P_{N}(n),

    where NN is the maximum allowed bag size.

  2. 2.

    Conditional on the bag size nn, the instances (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) are jointly drawn according to some distribution ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} on 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n}:

    (x1,…,xn)∼ℙn.(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}.

Therefore, the overall distribution of a bag B=(x1,…,xn)B=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) is

ℙ⁡(B)=PN​(n)⋅ℙn​(x1,…,xn),\mathbb{P}(B)=P_{N}(n)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),

where no independence assumption on the instances is made; they may follow an arbitrary joint distribution.

Definition F.4 (Bag cover set (Restated)).

Let S⊆𝒳S\subseteq\mathcal{X} be a set of instances. The bag cover set of SS is the set of all bags in ℬ\mathcal{B} that contain at least one instance from SS:

𝒞⁡(S):={B∈ℬ∣B∩S≠∅}.\mathcal{C}(S):=\{B\in\mathcal{B}\mid B\cap S\neq\emptyset\}.

That is, a bag BB belongs to 𝒞⁡(S)\mathcal{C}(S) if and only if it contains at least one instance from SS.

Similarly, we define the positive bag cover set and negative bag cover set of SS as follows:

𝒞+​(S):={B∈ℬ∣B∩S≠∅∧y⁡(B)=1};\mathcal{C}^{+}(S):=\{B\in\mathcal{B}\mid B\cap S\neq\emptyset\wedge y(B)=1\};
𝒞−​(S):={B∈ℬ∣B∩S≠∅∧y⁡(B)=0}.\mathcal{C}^{-}(S):=\{B\in\mathcal{B}\mid B\cap S\neq\emptyset\wedge y(B)=0\}.

A bag cover set 𝒞⁡(S)\mathcal{C}(S) (or 𝒞+​(S),𝒞−​(S)\mathcal{C}^{+}(S),\mathcal{C}^{-}(S)) is called non-trivial if its probability under the bag distribution ℙ\mathbb{P} is strictly positive:

ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))>0(or ​ℙ​(𝒞+​(S))>0,ℙ⁡(𝒞−​(S))>0).\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))>0\quad(\text{or }\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S))>0,\,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S))>0).
Assumption F.1 (MM-Assumption (Restated)).

There exists a constant M>0M>0 such that for any set of negative instances S⊆𝒳−S\subseteq\mathcal{X}^{-}, if

ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))=ℙ⁡(𝒞+​(S))+ℙ⁡(𝒞−​(S))>0,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S))+\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S))>0,

then

ℙ​(𝒞+​(S))ℙ​(𝒞−​(S))≤M,\frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S))}{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S))}\leq M,

where ℙ​(𝒞+​(S))\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S)) and ℙ​(𝒞−​(S))\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{-}(S)) denote the probabilities of the positive and negative bag cover sets under the bag distribution, respectively.

F.2 Mathematical Properties of Softmax Weight Sum

We first give a few lemmas about the mathematical properties of the Softmax Weight Sum (SWS) function.

Lemma F.1 (Partial derivative of SWS).

Let the temperature parameter be α>0\alpha>0 and let 𝐩=(p1,…,pn)∈[0,1]n\bm{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in[0,1]^{n}. Define the softmax weights wiw_{i} and the softmax weighted sum p^\hat{p} as

p^​(𝒑)=∑i=1nwi​pi,wi=epi/α∑j=1nepj/α.\hat{p}(\bm{p})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}p_{i},\qquad w_{i}=\frac{e^{p_{i}/\alpha}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{p_{j}/\alpha}}.

Then for any i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\} the partial derivative admits the representation

∂p^∂pi=wiα​(α+pi−p^).\frac{\partial\hat{p}}{\partial p_{i}}=\frac{w_{i}}{\alpha}\bigl(\alpha+p_{i}-\hat{p}\bigr).

In particular, the sign of the derivative is completely determined by the sign of (α+pi−p^)(\alpha+p_{i}-\hat{p}):

sgn⁡(∂p^∂pi)=sgn⁡(α+pi−p^).\operatorname{sgn}\left(\frac{\partial\hat{p}}{\partial p_{i}}\right)=\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\alpha+p_{i}-\hat{p}\bigr).

For any x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1), set ε=1−x>0\varepsilon=1-x>0. Applying Lemma F.4 with N=nN=n (the actual size of the bag) to the vector 𝒑=(x,p2,…,pn)\bm{p}=(x,p_{2},\dots,p_{n}) gives

≥δ⁡(ε,α,n)> 0.\displaystyle\geq\delta(\varepsilon,\alpha,n)\;>\;0.

F.3 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Lemma F.6 (Loss decrease for correcting false negatives).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the instance space, ℬ\mathcal{B} the bag space, and ℙ\mathbb{P} a distribution over ℬ\mathcal{B}. Let f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] be an instance-level classifier. For a bag B=(x1,…,xn)B=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) with label y⁡(B)∈{0,1}y(B)\in\{0,1\}, define the softmax weighted sum and the expected loss as

p^​(B)\displaystyle\hat{p}(B) =SWSα​(f⁡(x1),…,f⁡(xn)),\displaystyle=\mathrm{SWS}_{\alpha}\bigl(f(x_{1}),\dots,f(x_{n})\bigr),

Let S+⊆𝒳+S^{+}\subseteq\mathcal{X}^{+} be a set of positive instances satisfying ℙ⁡(𝒞+​(S+))>0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}^{+}(S^{+}))>0, and assume f⁡(x)<1f(x)<1 for all x∈S+x\in S^{+}. Define a new classifier f′f^{\prime} by

>0,\displaystyle>0,

Combining the four terms. If ℙ⁡(A1∪A2)>0\mathbb{P}(A_{1}\cup A_{2})>0, we already have Δ1+Δ2>0\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}>0 while Δ3,Δ4≥0\Delta_{3},\Delta_{4}\geq 0, so the sum is strictly positive. Theorem F.8 (Unique global minimizer (Restated)).

Let 𝒳,ℬ,ℙ,p^,ℒ\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B},\mathbb{P},\hat{p},\mathcal{L} be as defined in Lemma F.6. Suppose that Assumption F.1 (the MM-assumption) holds. Let NN be the maximum bag size, u=W0​(N−1e)u=W_{0}\!\bigl(\frac{N-1}{e}\bigr), and MM the constant from that assumption. Then there exists a sufficiently small temperature α>0\alpha>0 such that, up to a set of instances SS whose bag cover set has probability zero, ℒ\mathcal{L} is uniquely minimized by the true label function:

f∗​(x)=y⁡(x)∈{0,1},∀x∉S.f^{*}(x)=y(x)\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall x\notin S.

Equivalently, any global minimiser f∗f^{*} must satisfy f∗​(x)=y​(x)f^{*}(x)=y(x) for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, except possibly on a set S⊆𝒳S\subseteq\mathcal{X} with ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))=0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))=0.

Proof.

Choose the temperature α>0\alpha>0 such that

α<12​(u+1),−log⁡(α⁡(2​u+1))+M​log⁡(1−α​u)>0.\begin{split}&\alpha<\frac{1}{2(u+1)},\\ &-\log\!\bigl(\alpha(2u+1)\bigr)+M\log(1-\alpha u)>0.\end{split} (9)

Such α\alpha exists because the left-hand side of the second inequality tends to +∞+\infty as α→0+\alpha\to 0^{+}, while the first is an explicit positive upper bound. We fix this α\alpha for the remainder of the proof; note that it depends only on NN and MM.

Let ff be any global minimiser of ℒ\mathcal{L}. We show that ff must coincide with the true labels everywhere except on a set with zero bag-cover probability.

Step 1. Correction of false negatives. Set S+:={x∈𝒳+∣f⁡(x)<1}S^{+}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}^{+}\mid f(x)<1\}. If ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S+))>0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S^{+}))>0, then Lemma F.6 (which holds for any α>0\alpha>0, in particular for our chosen α\alpha) applied to S+S^{+} produces f1​(x)=1f_{1}(x)=1 for x∈S+x\in S^{+}, f1​(x)=f​(x)f_{1}(x)=f(x) otherwise, with ℒ⁡(f1)<ℒ⁡(f)\mathcal{L}(f_{1})<\mathcal{L}(f), contradicting optimality. Hence ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S+))=0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S^{+}))=0.

Because the bag cover of S+S^{+} has probability zero, modifying ff on S+S^{+} does not change the expected loss. Define

f~​(x):={1,x∈𝒳+,f⁡(x),x∈𝒳−.\tilde{f}(x):=\begin{cases}1,&x\in\mathcal{X}^{+},\\ f(x),&x\in\mathcal{X}^{-}.\end{cases}

Then ℒ⁡(f~)=ℒ⁡(f)\mathcal{L}(\tilde{f})=\mathcal{L}(f), so f~\tilde{f} is also a global minimiser.

Step 2. Correction of false positives. Consider the negative instances where f~\tilde{f} is strictly positive: S−:={x∈𝒳−∣f~​(x)>0}S^{-}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}^{-}\mid\tilde{f}(x)>0\}. If ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S−))=0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S^{-}))=0, the claim already holds with S=S+∪S−S=S^{+}\cup S^{-}. Assume therefore ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S−))>0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S^{-}))>0. By construction, f~\tilde{f} satisfies exactly the hypotheses of Lemma F.7: f~​(x)=1\tilde{f}(x)=1 on 𝒳+\mathcal{X}^{+}, f~​(x)∈(0,1]\tilde{f}(x)\in(0,1] on S−S^{-}, and f~​(x)=0\tilde{f}(x)=0 on 𝒳−∖S−\mathcal{X}^{-}\setminus S^{-}. Moreover, our chosen α\alpha fulfills the two inequalities that are shown (in the proof of Lemma F.7) to be sufficient for the strict decrease of the loss when the false positives in S−S^{-} are set to 00. Consequently, the same construction applied to f~\tilde{f} and S−S^{-} with temperature α\alpha yields a classifier

f~′​(x)={0,x∈S−,f~​(x),otherwise,\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in S^{-},\\ \tilde{f}(x),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

satisfying ℒ⁡(f~′)<ℒ⁡(f~)\mathcal{L}(\tilde{f}^{\prime})<\mathcal{L}(\tilde{f}). This contradicts the global optimality of f~\tilde{f} (and hence of ff). Thus ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S−))=0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S^{-}))=0 as well.

Conclusion. Let S=S+∪S−S=S^{+}\cup S^{-}. We have ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))=0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))=0. For x∉Sx\notin S, if x∈𝒳+x\in\mathcal{X}^{+} then f⁡(x)=1f(x)=1 (otherwise xx would belong to S+S^{+}), and if x∈𝒳−x\in\mathcal{X}^{-} then f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 (otherwise x∈S−x\in S^{-}). Thus f⁡(x)=y⁡(x)f(x)=y(x) for all x∉Sx\notin S, which is exactly the statement of the theorem. ∎

F.4 Proof of Theorem 3.2

Lemma F.9 (Quantitative loss decrease for correcting false negatives).

Let α>0\alpha>0 and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} (N≥1N\geq 1) be the temperature and maximum bag size. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X}, ℬ\mathcal{B}, ℙ\mathbb{P}, p^​(⋅)\hat{p}(\cdot) and ℒ\mathcal{L} be as in Lemma F.6. ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f′)≥δ⋅ΛFN​(ε,α,N)> 0,\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f^{\prime})\;\geq\;\delta\cdot\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}(\varepsilon,\alpha,N)\;>\;0,

where

ΛFN​(ε,α,N)=log\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}(\varepsilon,\alpha,N)=\log
(1+min⁡{11+(N−1)​e1/α,ε1+(N−1)​eε/α}).\displaystyle\left(1+\min\!\left\{\frac{1}{1+(N-1)e^{1/\alpha}},\;\frac{\varepsilon}{1+(N-1)e^{\varepsilon/\alpha}}\right\}\right).

δ0\displaystyle\delta_{0} =min⁡{11+(N−1)​e1/α,ε1+(N−1)​eε/α}\displaystyle=\min\!\left\{\frac{1}{1+(N-1)e^{1/\alpha}},\;\frac{\varepsilon}{1+(N-1)e^{\varepsilon/\alpha}}\right\}
>0.\displaystyle>0.

Lemma F.10 (Quantitative loss decrease for correcting false positives).

Let 𝒳,ℬ,ℙ,p^,ℒ\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B},\mathbb{P},\hat{p},\mathcal{L} be as in Lemma F.6. Suppose Assumption F.1 (the MM-assumption) holds. where ΛFP​(ε,α,N,M)=\Lambda_{\mathrm{FP}}(\varepsilon,\alpha,N,M)=

11+M⋅min{\displaystyle\frac{1}{1+M}\cdot\min\Bigl\{ −log⁡(α⁡(2​u+1))+M​log⁡(1−α​u),\displaystyle-\log\!\bigl(\alpha(2u+1)\bigr)+M\log(1-\alpha u),

Theorem F.11 (Convergence in probability (Restated)).

Let Assumption 3.1 hold. Let NN be the maximum allowed bag size, u=W0​(N−1e)u=W_{0}\bigl(\frac{N-1}{e}\bigr), and MM the constant from the MM-assumption. Let f∗​(x)=y​(x)f^{*}(x)=y(x) be the Bayes optimal classifier, and let {fl}\{f_{l}\} be a sequence of instance classifiers. Define the expected loss ℒ⁡(f)\mathcal{L}(f) as in Lemma F.6. Then there exists a sufficiently small temperature α>0\alpha>0 such that, if liml→∞ℒ⁡(fl)=ℒ⁡(f∗)\lim_{l\to\infty}\mathcal{L}(f_{l})=\mathcal{L}(f^{*}), then {fl}\{f_{l}\} converges to f∗f^{*} in probability. Equivalently, for any ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0,

liml→∞ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡({x:|fl​(x)−f∗​(x)|≥ε}))=0.\lim_{l\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\mathcal{C}\bigl(\{x:|f_{l}(x)-f^{*}(x)|\geq\varepsilon\}\bigr)\Bigr)=0.
Proof.

Choose a temperature α>0\alpha>0 small enough to satisfy both

α\displaystyle\alpha <12​(u+1),\displaystyle<\frac{1}{2(u+1)}, (14)
Λ0\displaystyle\Lambda_{0} :=−log⁡(α⁡(2​u+1))+M​log⁡(1−α​u)>0.\displaystyle:=-\log\!\bigl(\alpha(2u+1)\bigr)+M\log(1-\alpha u)>0.

Such α\alpha exists because Λ0→+∞\Lambda_{0}\to+\infty as α→0+\alpha\to 0^{+} while the first bound is an explicit positive constant. In the sequel we work with this fixed α\alpha. Define the two positive constants

Λ1​(ε)\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon) :=ΛFN​(ε,α,N),\displaystyle:=\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}(\varepsilon,\alpha,N),
Λ2​(ε)\displaystyle\Lambda_{2}(\varepsilon) :=ΛFP​(ε,α,N,M),\displaystyle:=\Lambda_{\mathrm{FP}}(\varepsilon,\alpha,N,M),

where ΛFN\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}} and ΛFP\Lambda_{\mathrm{FP}} are given by Lemma F.9 and Lemma F.10 respectively. Both Λ1​(ε)\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon) and Λ2​(ε)\Lambda_{2}(\varepsilon) are strictly positive for every ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1].

Fix arbitrary ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0 and set

ξ:=δ⋅min⁡{Λ1​(ε),Λ2​(ε)}>0.\xi:=\delta\cdot\min\{\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon),\,\Lambda_{2}(\varepsilon)\}>0.

ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡({x:|f⁡(x)−f∗​(x)|≥ε}))≥δ\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\mathcal{C}\bigl(\{x:|f(x)-f^{*}(x)|\geq\varepsilon\}\bigr)\Bigr)\geq\delta (15)
⟹ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f∗)≥ξ.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f^{*})\geq\xi.

Once this implication is proved, the convergence follows immediately: if ℒ⁡(fl)→ℒ⁡(f∗)\mathcal{L}(f_{l})\to\mathcal{L}(f^{*}), then for sufficiently large ll we have ℒ⁡(fl)−ℒ⁡(f∗)<ξ\mathcal{L}(f_{l})-\mathcal{L}(f^{*})<\xi, which forces the left-hand side of (15) to be smaller than δ\delta. Hence the bag-cover probability of the ε\varepsilon-deviating instances tends to 00.

Proof of (15). Let ff be a classifier with ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))≥δ\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))\geq\delta, where S:={x:|f⁡(x)−f∗​(x)|≥ε}S:=\{x:|f(x)-f^{*}(x)|\geq\varepsilon\}. Decompose SS into false negatives and false positives:

SFP\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{FP}} :={x∈𝒳−:f⁡(x)≥ε}.\displaystyle:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}^{-}:f(x)\geq\varepsilon\}.

Clearly S=SFN∪SFPS=S_{\mathrm{FN}}\cup S_{\mathrm{FP}} and the union is disjoint. Denote δ1=ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(SFN))\delta_{1}=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S_{\mathrm{FN}})) and δ2=ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(SFP))\delta_{2}=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S_{\mathrm{FP}})). By subadditivity of ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(⋅))\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(\cdot)),

δ≤ℙ⁡(𝒞⁡(S))≤δ1+δ2.\delta\leq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}(S))\leq\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}.

We now modify ff to the Bayes classifier f∗f^{*} in three steps and track the loss decrease.

ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f1)≥δ1​Λ1​(ε).\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f_{1})\;\geq\;\delta_{1}\,\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon).

If δ1=0\delta_{1}=0 the inequality trivially holds as 0≥00\geq 0.

Step 2: Correct remaining false negatives. Define f2f_{2} by f2​(x)=1f_{2}(x)=1 for all x∈𝒳+x\in\mathcal{X}^{+} and f2​(x)=f1​(x)f_{2}(x)=f_{1}(x) for x∈𝒳−x\in\mathcal{X}^{-}. ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f2)≥δ1​Λ1​(ε).\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f_{2})\;\geq\;\delta_{1}\,\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon).

Step 3: Correct false positives. Now f2f_{2} satisfies precisely the prerequisites of Lemma F.10: f2​(x)=1f_{2}(x)=1 on 𝒳+\mathcal{X}^{+}, f2​(x)∈(0,1]f_{2}(x)\in(0,1] on S−:={x∈𝒳−:f2​(x)>0}S^{-}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}^{-}:f_{2}(x)>0\}, and f2​(x)=0f_{2}(x)=0 on the rest of 𝒳−\mathcal{X}^{-}. The set SFPS_{\mathrm{FP}} is exactly S~\tilde{S} in that lemma, and its bag-cover probability is δ2\delta_{2}. Applying Lemma F.10 with the already chosen α\alpha (which satisfies (14)) gives

ℒ⁡(f2)−ℒ⁡(f′)≥δ2​Λ2​(ε),\mathcal{L}(f_{2})-\mathcal{L}(f^{\prime})\;\geq\;\delta_{2}\,\Lambda_{2}(\varepsilon),

where f′f^{\prime} is the classifier obtained by setting all instances in S−S^{-} to 00. Note that f′f^{\prime} assigns 11 to all positive instances and 00 to all negative ones, i.e. f′=f∗f^{\prime}=f^{*}. Hence ℒ⁡(f′)=ℒ⁡(f∗)\mathcal{L}(f^{\prime})=\mathcal{L}(f^{*}).

≥(δ1+δ2)​min⁡{Λ1​(ε),Λ2​(ε)}\displaystyle\;\geq\;(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2})\,\min\{\Lambda_{1}(\varepsilon),\Lambda_{2}(\varepsilon)\}
